title: After 300 episodes, Willy Walker answers the questions
summary: Carol McNerney reflects on Willy Walker’s candid conversation with Evan Osnos about risk, mistakes, leadership, and lessons learned.
body_markdown:
For 300 episodes of the[Walker Webcast](https://www.walkerdunlop.com/webcast) , Willy Walker has asked the questions. Journalist and author Evan Osnos turned the tables for this milestone episode.


The conversation covered Walker & Dunlop, commercial real estate, artificial intelligence, and some of the memorable guests Willy has interviewed. But some of the most revealing moments came when Evan asked Willy to look back at decisions he had made, mistakes he had learned from, and ways his thinking has changed.


## You can’t do everything


Early in the conversation, Evan asked Willy a question many people have probably wondered: How does he fit everything into his life?


Willy’s answer was not about time management. He went back to 2012. Walker & Dunlop had recently gone public. He had three sons under 10, chaired three public company boards, and decided to train for the Olympic-distance triathlon national championships. He finished fourth.


“When you pack that much into your life at one time, something is going to break,” he said. For Willy, his marriage was what broke. He recently shared the same story with students at the University of Michigan, where he encouraged them to move away from always trying to be the “best, fastest, smartest” and toward “living, being, loving.”


Anyone who knows Willy knows how competitive he is. He hasn’t lost his competitive fire. Experience has given him a clearer view of where it can take you, along with what can get lost along the way.


## Some lessons require a change of course


The end of Willy’s marriage also forced him to examine his relationship with his sons. He realized he had been raising them to become the people he wanted them to be rather than giving them room to become the people they wanted to be.


Willy changed how he parented. He returned to the value of acknowledging mistakes when he talked about his recent visit to Michigan. He had gone there to discuss real estate, cap rates, and the housing market. The students became more engaged when he began talking about things he had gotten wrong, personally and professionally.


Success stories tend to become cleaner with time. The mistakes, detours, and difficult decisions disappear, leaving a straight line between where someone started and where they ended up. Willy’s account was considerably less tidy.


## Risk looks different in retrospect


Evan also pressed Willy on risk. Willy described several points in Walker & Dunlop’s history when the company made unusually consequential bets. One involved a 2012 acquisition in which three bankers represented a significant share of the company’s revenue. Walker & Dunlop had to proceed without knowing whether those bankers would come with the deal. They did, and the acquisition helped transform the company.


Willy also talked about an acquisition he chose not to make and later regretted. The two stories belong together. One risk paid off. One opportunity passed by. Neither outcome was obvious when the decision had to be made.


Willy described the challenge as knowing when to lean in and when to back off. “There’s no course on that at university,” he said. Experience fills in some of the curriculum.


## Curiosity is still doing a lot of the work


When Evan turned to the Walker Webcast itself, Willy talked about what he has learned from interviewing hundreds of people.


Preparation is a big part of it. Willy recalled watching David Rubenstein conduct interviews without notes and realizing how thoroughly Rubenstein had prepared beforehand. Willy adopted a similar approach: Learn enough about the person sitting across from you to get beyond the standard questions.


Regular viewers have seen where that approach can lead. A conversation about a book can become a discussion about how a novelist thinks. An interview with a military leader can return to a decision made decades earlier. A conversation with an athlete can move well beyond sports.


Willy reads widely, asks plenty of questions, and stays genuinely interested in what other people know. After 300 episodes, curiosity may be one of the simplest explanations for the webcast’s staying power.


## Turning the questions around


A 300th episode could easily have become a retrospective of favorite guests, big moments, and milestones. Evan went in another direction.


He asked Willy what he has learned, where he has been wrong, what he would do differently, and what might come next. He even worked in questions about hockey, Burning Man, and the book Willy may someday write.


Mostly, Evan gave Willy the kind of interview Willy has spent five years trying to give his guests: one that gets beyond the résumé and into the experiences behind it.


For once, Willy had to answer the questions, and there was plenty worth hearing.


[Watch the full Walker Webcast](https://www.walkerdunlop.com/webcast/episodes/willy-walker-300th-episode) with Willy Walker and Evan Osnos.
